builder_plan.scenario: An agent looks good in demos, but you cannot tell which product tasks it fails.
builder_plan.change: Use the study's evaluation idea to inspect a small set of tasks with human-checked answers.
builder_plan.baseline: Your current evaluator and a manually reviewed reference set.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Agreement with human review, missed failures, false alarms, and evaluation cost per task.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: AIChipBench: Benchmarking LLM Agents for Automated AI Accelerator Design
summary: AIChipBench replaces ad hoc or output-only evaluation of LLM coding agents for hardware design with an executable integer reference that exposes stored-state mismatches at every decoding step, plus held-out grading on new token sequences, resets, memory stalls, and synthesis. It costs the effort of building step-level reference state and substantially expanded final test suites rather than relying on public output tests, and it does not itself provide an adoptable tool or model. The demonstrated failure mode is directly relevant to agent evaluation generally: designs pass output tests while corrupting internal state, with 45 of 69 accepted designs failing under regrading, so any agentic workflow the reader adopts should use state-level or intermediate feedback and final tests well beyond development cases.
rationale: The paper is a benchmark and methodology study for LLM agents that design hardware RTL, a task outside the reader's production scope, though its findings on state-exposing feedback and held-out grading generalize to any evaluation of coding agents.
technique: State-exposing benchmark for LLM hardware-design agents

claims.statement: AIChipBench replaces ad hoc or output-only evaluation of LLM coding agents for hardware design with an executable integer reference that exposes stored-state mismatches at every decoding step, plus held-out grading on new token sequences, resets, memory stalls, and synthesis. It costs the effort of building step-level reference state and substantially expanded final test suites rather than relying on public output tests, and it does not itself provide an adoptable tool or model. The demonstrated failure mode is directly relevant to agent evaluation generally: designs pass output tests while corrupting internal state, with 45 of 69 accepted designs failing under regrading, so any agentic workflow the reader adopts should use state-level or intermediate feedback and final tests well beyond development cases.

Feedback pointing to the first state mismatch raises agent acceptance rates by 25.0 to 46.9 percentage points over output-only feedback across all 12 agent-task cells, and halves agent-hours per accepted design; 45 of 69 accepted designs fail when regraded on held-out sequences and conditions.
